name: Rafael Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Danby's, a free-range egg farm with four sheds of laying hens, about thirty-two thousand birds, and some fields of wheat the Danbys grow for their own feed. I start at six, walk every shed, pick up any dead birds, check the water lines and the feeders, and then open the pop-holes so the hens can go out. Afternoons I'm in the packing room or on the tractor in the wheat. I've been there two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is the first walk in the morning, when it's quiet and the birds are just waking up and I know every noise in that shed. The hard bit is bird flu season, when everything's shut in and you're in a paper suit for hours and Mr Danby's on edge. I'm also still not great at spotting a sick bird early. Leon, who's been there twelve years, can see it from the door.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've never used one and I don't really plan to. My sister keeps telling me to, she's in marketing, but I like knowing where my answers come from. I've got a phone, it does calls and the weather, that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing much changes, carry on. At the pub I'd say I don't use it and I'm doing fine. I'm not really one for saying things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing for me, and I'm glad. Hens lay at the same rate whatever's on someone's computer. If anything I'd worry Mr Danby gets some new app and wants me to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same as now. Keep learning from Leon, get better at spotting the sick ones. I'd keep my savings in the building society like they are, I'm not touching that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's my favourite kind of year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you tell me about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Pete left me some money when he died, and I've added to it since. It's about a year and a half of wages. I'm careful with it, because it's the only reason I sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Danby did bring in an app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn it, slowly, and grumble. He brought in an automatic feeder controller last year with a screen, and it took me a month to stop phoning Leon about it. I'm not proud of that, but I got there.

S0.say: I'd say nothing much changes, so carry on. At the pub I'd say I don't use AI and I'm doing fine, but I wouldn't say anything online.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me, and I'm glad, because hens lay the same either way. My only worry is Mr Danby buying some new app I'd have to learn.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and learns from Leon to spot sick birds earlier. Leaves his savings untouched in the building society.
S0.feel: Calm, which he calls his favourite kind of year.
S0.quote: Hens lay at the same rate whatever's on someone's computer.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is quiet and steady, and his savings from an uncle are clearly what lets him relax. He admits it took a month to learn the feeder controller. His views are middle-of-the-road and he doesn't blame anyone in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for young people, and I'd mean it, but I'd also say farms have always hired fewer people every year. My granddad's farm had nine men. That's just how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad I'm already in. If I'd had to find a farm job in that world, with my skill level, I'm not sure I'd have got one. That's a bit frightening to think about, even though it's already behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do anything big. I'd make sure I'm useful to Mr Danby, take on the shed nobody likes, which is shed four, the old one. And I'd keep my savings exactly where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Like hearing about a car crash on a road you drove yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does nobody like shed four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the oldest and the ventilation's bad, so in summer it's like walking into soup. The egg belt jams there more than anywhere. But if I'm the one who keeps it running, I'm harder to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farms have always hired fewer people. Do you blame anyone for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Supermarkets push the egg price down, so farms buy machines. The government could help more, but so could the supermarkets. I don't like picking one person to blame, it's usually a bit of everyone.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people, but farms have always hired fewer people each year. My granddad's farm had nine men, and that's just how it goes.
S1.think: I'm privately glad I'm already in, because with my skill level I'm not sure I'd get a farm job in that world. It's frightening to think about, even though it's behind me.
S1.do: Makes himself useful by taking on shed four, the oldest shed nobody wants, and keeps the egg belt running there. Leaves his savings exactly where they are.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like hearing of a crash on a road he drove yesterday.
S1.quote: Like hearing about a car crash on a road you drove yesterday.
S1.fieldNote: His plan is to make himself hard to let go by taking the worst shed, which is a quiet, practical kind of strategy. He spreads the blame across supermarkets and government. He's honest that his own route in might be closed to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough on office people, and the government should help them a bit, but not hand out money for nothing. Something in the middle, like help with retraining. I'd probably say it to my sister, since she'd be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think it touches me at all. Nobody's going to send an AI into shed four. My worry would be my sister Ana, who writes adverts for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Danby's and tell Ana she can borrow from me if she needs to. I'd probably keep a bit more in my current account, just in case she does. At work, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Ana, fine for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you lend her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever she needs for rent while she sorts herself out, up to a few months. She lent me money for my first car, so it's only fair. I'd not ask for it back in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this picture make you more open to trying AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. If anything, the opposite. Watching it take my sister's job would make me want even less to do with it.

S2.say: I'd say it's tough on office workers and the government should help with retraining, but not hand out money for nothing. I'd mostly say it to my sister, since she'd be one of them.
S2.think: I don't think it touches me, because nobody will send an AI into shed four. My worry would be my sister Ana, who writes adverts.
S2.do: Carries on at Danby's and offers Ana a loan to cover a few months' rent. Keeps more money in his current account so it's ready if she needs it.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Ana, fine for himself.
S2.quote: Watching it take my sister's job would make me want even less to do with it.
S2.fieldNote: His centre views come out as help, but not too much help, and his family loyalty is strong. Seeing his sister hurt would make him even less willing to try AI. The loan to Ana repays an old favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something has to be sorted out about who gets the money, but I'd not go on marches about it. I'd say both sides need to calm down and find a deal. People losing jobs need help, and people who did well can afford a bit more tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay. My job's physical, so it's safe in this one, and my savings would be fine. But I'd hate the mood of it all, with everyone angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at work, do my shifts, and maybe pick up extra hours if anyone leaves. I'd stay away from shares, because I don't understand them and booms end. I'd help Ana if she lost her job, which in this one she probably would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe, but in a country that's arguing all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this where you'd be tempted to buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not at boom prices. I'd wait. My uncle used to say, never buy when everyone else is buying, and he did all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Danby's would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, in this one. Mrs Danby does the books, and maybe an AI could do that, but she's family. If anyone, it's the woman at the feed company who rings with our orders, she's lovely, and she'd be gone.

S3.say: I'd say someone needs to sort out who gets the money, and both sides should calm down and find a deal. People who lost jobs need help, and those who did well can afford a bit more tax.
S3.think: Privately I'd be okay, because my physical job is safe and my savings are fine. I'd just hate the mood of it, with everyone angry.
S3.do: Keeps his head down, works his shifts and picks up extra hours if anyone leaves. Avoids shares and boom-price houses, and stands ready to help Ana.
S3.feel: Uneasy, safe himself but living in a country that argues all the time.
S3.quote: Never buy when everyone else is buying, and he did all right.
S3.fieldNote: Rafael wants calm more than any particular outcome. He leans on his late uncle's advice about money. The only person he'd worry about at work is the friendly woman at the feed company, which shows how little this picture reaches the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow it down, there's no need to rush robots onto every farm. I'd say farmers should have a say, and so should the people working on them. I'm not against machines, but this is too much, too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one I'd lose sleep over. The hens already lay onto a belt. The only thing on this farm that isn't a machine is me. A robot that can walk the sheds and pick up dead birds would do my whole morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Danby straight out what his plans are, the first week the robots are in the farming magazines. If he says he's buying one, I'd start looking for work in something robots can't do yet, but I honestly don't know what that is. I'd stop spending on anything extra and keep the savings as a runway, maybe a year and a half if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. Like the floor's moved and nobody told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for work robots can't do yet. What comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe fixing the robots, but that's tech and I'm bad at tech. Maybe something with people, like care work, but the card says robots go there too. That's what scares me, there's no obvious next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run the robot if Mr Danby asked you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try. I'd hate it, and I'd be slow, like with the feeder screen. But a month of phoning Leon is better than no job.

S4.say: I'd say slow it down, because there's no need to rush robots onto every farm. Farmers and their workers should have a say, and while I'm not against machines, this is too much too fast.
S4.think: This is the one I'd lose sleep over, because the hens already lay onto a belt. The only thing on this farm that isn't a machine is me, and a shed-walking robot would do my whole morning.
S4.do: Asks Mr Danby about his robot plans in the first week they make the farming magazines. Cuts all extra spending to keep about a year and a half of savings as a runway, and agrees to try learning the robot if asked.
S4.feel: Properly worried, as if the floor moved and nobody told him.
S4.quote: The hens already lay onto a belt. The only thing on this farm that isn't a machine is me.
S4.fieldNote: A big jump from uneasy to alarmed. He has the savings to wait, but no idea what work he'd move to, and that blank is what frightens him. He'd still try to learn the robot, slowly, which shows more give than his first answers suggested.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one. The rest I can watch from shed four, but that one comes into the shed. What would help is time, honestly, a rule that farms phase robots in slowly so people can see it coming, and a straight answer from the boss about what's planned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be bad at the thing everyone says is the future. People keep telling me to learn AI like it's easy. For some of us it isn't, and that should count for something.

headlineQuote: The only thing on this farm that isn't a machine is me.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old junior on a free-range egg farm who loves the quiet first walk through the sheds and is still learning to spot a sick bird the way his colleague Leon can. He never uses AI, keeps a year and a half of savings from his late uncle in the building society, and takes advice from that uncle about not buying in a boom. His views are centrist: help people, but not too much, and don't blame one side. He's calm through the office pictures, worrying mainly about his sister Ana in advertising, until the robot picture, where he sees himself as the last non-machine on an already automated farm and has no idea what work he'd move to.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it comes right into the shed and he can't see an obvious next step for himself.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that farms bring robots in slowly so people can see it coming, and a straight answer from his boss about the plans.
